newsitem.title: UK: Bond yields could creep up post-EMU - EC's Carre.
newsitem.headline: Bond yields could creep up post-EMU - EC's Carre.

text.p: Bond yields could rise in the short term after European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) begins on January 1, 1999, a top European Commission (EC) official said on Thursday.

"The absolute level of bond yields will largely depend on the expectations regarding monetary policy," Herve Carre, director for monetary matters at the European Commission, told a conference on EMU in London.

He said the European Central Bank's (ECB) independence, its obligation laid down in the Maastricht Treaty to maintain price stability and the high degree of bond conversion already achieved, should lead to low bond yields.

"However, market confidence will have to be confirmed by actual implimentation of monetary policy of the ECB. In the short term it could imply somewhat higher money market rates than necessary," he said.
But the EMU stability pact would soon reduce this risk.
Carre said the fact a great bulk of financial activity will switch into euros at the start of EMU in 1999 will help to confirm its irreversibility and give a boost to the euro bond market.
Carre said bond markets under EMU will become a single, deeper, wider and more resilient market.
He said combined EU member state bond markets are around 60 percent of the US Treasury market in size and bigger than Japan.
"It can become a competitor of the US. dollar market," he said.
There remains the question of which country would play the role of benchmark for European bond markets, he said.
"The market that offers a complete range of interest rates, and deep liquidity will be in a better position to become the benchmark," he said.
